title: Zen and Conflict
speaker: Yuzan Nancy Welch
summary: Yuzan Nancy Welch's main teaching is that when we're in conflict with others, our reactions are often driven by fear and a desire to control or fix the situation, which only leads to further conflict. Instead, they suggest focusing on understanding the present moment and the other person's intentions, rather than getting caught up in strong emotions or trying to change them. By letting go of our need to correct others and instead approaching the situation with curiosity and compassion, we can respond more thoughtfully and peacefully, even in difficult situations.

sentences.text: Tonight I'd like to talk about Zen and working with conflicts, especially as it pertains to our sangha.

I know next week after this evening meditation we're going to have an open sangha meeting for people to discuss some of the changes in forms and things that have gone on the past few months and things like that.
I've been with this group a long time, and what I've noticed is that changes like that can be very profound in how they affect different people, even the smallest change.
Different people react differently.

Some people, like me, if I don't like it, I tend to ignore it, which is the best way to be, but I guess that's how I used to get full of righteous indignation about things, but I don't get that way so much anymore.
But other people feel very strong feelings about it, and so I've been pondering this the past few weeks because some people have talked to me about it.
It seems to me that at the root of conflicts, all conflicts, whether it be between friends, husband and wife, sangha members, the root is fear.
And I'm drawing from a couple different sources tonight.
One is our teacher, guiding teacher Norman, taking our places.
He talks about, well, in here he says, he states in Buddhism, all spiritual practice is like a tripod.
It has three strong legs that hold us upright, steady, and firm.
And those three legs are ethical conduct, meditation, and wisdom.
Well, for wisdom, I'm hoping that will come in time.
Meditation is, and probably always will be difficult for me and my body, but it is critical for this practice.
Ethical conduct.
Now this is where, so I don't disagree with those two, but I don't really disagree with ethical conduct, but I think ethical conduct is what stirs up the most controversy.
What's ethical conduct to me might not be considered ethical by someone else.
We have the precepts to guide us, and one that particularly pertains here is the sixth precept, and that is not discussing the faults of others.
Like I said, ethical conduct is where I have always had very strong opinions.
I don't know if that's how it is for you, but I have always thought I knew how others should behave, and what I know is right, and I don't understand why other people don't get it.
So the conduct of others has been an issue for me for a very long time, and as I said, I often used to respond with a lot of righteous indignation.
I was one of those placard carriers out in the street.
But more personally, when I see someone, either on a personal level or national level, but we won't go there anymore, he's gone.
When I see somebody doing something that I think is wrong or mean or thoughtless or just self-serving, I really want to put a stop to it.
I want to inform that person just what it is they're doing wrong and what they need to do to make it right, make amends, or at least just make me feel better anyway.
But I usually don't do that.
I don't go to that person because it's scary, as some of you may feel.
It's scary to go up to somebody and say, you know, I think you're wrong about this.
It's scary because they might not like it.
They might get mad.
They might laugh at me and tell me I'm being stupid, or they might not like me anymore.
All those are kind of scary things to think about.
And so I think my tendency, as I've seen in others too, is that when we consider all those possible horrible things that could come, we make a decision not to go to that person.
What I do is I keep it in for a while.
I tell myself, well, I just tuck it up, let it fester a little bit, and maybe tell myself I am so above all this that I would not stoop to criticizing.
Bam, there goes precept number seven.
But eventually I have to tell someone.
I mean, what's the point of being so good if nobody knows about it, right?

So I go tell someone, usually someone who I figure will be on my side, and I make all the brilliant arguments for why I am so right and the other person is so wrong, and I try to get everybody on my side, and I feel good about that for a while.
Joko Beck, in her book *Everyday Zen*, has some really entertaining things to say about this.
I'll just read you one or two here.
She talks about conflict as she gives this sort of analogy.
Suppose we're out on a lake and it's a bit foggy, not too foggy, but a bit, and we're rowing along in our little boat having a good time.
Then all of a sudden, coming out of the fog, there's this other rowboat and it's heading right at us, and crash.
Well, for a second we're really angry.
What is that fool doing?
I just painted my boat, and here he comes, bam, right into it.
Idiot, can't he see?
And then suddenly we notice the rowboat's empty.
So what happens to our anger?
Well, the anger collapses.
I think I'll just have to paint my boat again, that's all.
But if that rowboat that hit us had another person in it, how would we react?
How would we feel?
You know what would happen?
Now our encounters with life, with other people, with events, are a lot like being bumped by an empty rowboat, if we can see it that way.
But we don't experience life that way.
We experience it as though there are people in that other rowboat and we're really getting clobbered by them.
What am I talking about when I say that all of life is an encounter, a collision with an empty boat?
What's that all about?
I think it's about how we tend to respond when somebody, well, what we think is somebody, some person, something, is getting in our way.
Another example, she says, let's take a quarrel at breakfast.

At lunchtime we're still upset, not only upset, but we've begun telling everybody about it, getting comfort, sympathy, agreement, and already we're in our heads thinking, when I get home tonight, we're going to discuss this.
We are really going to get at this matter.
So you have the breakfast quarrel, the luncheon upset, and then there's the future.
What are we going to do about this upset?
What is really here?
What's really now?
As we sit having our lunch, where is that breakfast quarrel?
Where is it?
It says in some of the Zen readings, the mind of the past is ungraspable.
But where is it in the dinner when we're really going to fix this?
To our satisfaction, of course.
Where is it?
Because the mind of the future is ungraspable.
It doesn't exist.
So what does exist?
What's real?
There is just my upset right now at breakfast, at lunch.
My story describing what happened at breakfast is not what happened.
It's my story.
What is real is the headache, the stomach churning, and my chattering is a manifestation of that physical energy.
Outside of the physical experience there is nothing else that's real.
And I don't know if that's real, but that's all we can say about it.
She gives one other example that's pretty funny.
A woman not a Zen student came to her to complain about her husband.
She was really, really upset.
She could hardly speak.
And so when Joko Beck said, well, where is your husband right now?
She said, well, he's at work.
Joko Beck said, well, where is this upset, this quarrel you're talking about?
Where is it?
Can you show me?
Well, I'm telling you about it, the woman said.
I can't show you, but I'm telling you about it.
See, this is the way it was.
But when was it?
I asked her.
Three weeks ago?
Okay, so where is it?
So she was getting more and more annoyed, and finally she could see that none of the upset had any reality whatsoever.
And then she said, but if that's all there is, how can I make my husband change?
So yeah, I think we all do some form of this.
And we'll most likely, I know for myself, continue to do this.

But hopefully, as we become more aware of what we are doing, what I am doing, as opposed to heightening my awareness of what a screw up so-and-so is, maybe there can be a shift from anger to understanding, or at least trying to understand what that other person is thinking, feeling, what are their real intentions?
Are they really out to get me?
Perhaps a shift from pride, which is my righteous anger, to humility.

And I don't mean humiliation, but a happy, funny kind of humility where I can laugh at myself for getting all worked up and taking someone's behavior so personally, and then trying to get everyone on my side, line up my arguments, and prove to the world why I'm right and that other person is a big fat idiot.
What a lot of energy.
So once I'm aware of this rather unproductive way of coping with conflict, what can I do to change it?
This is a fun book, *Destructive Emotions*.
It's a dialogue between the Dalai Lama and a whole bunch of scientists, psychologists, and I'd like to just pull out one excerpt here where he's talking with a psychologist, Paul Ekman.
Sorry for those of you named Tim, but this is called The Case of Teasable Tim.
Suppose a boy, who I'll call Tim, was teased by a cruel father whose teases were made as a joke, but their cruel edge was to mock and humiliate.
When Tim would get upset when his father teased him, that delighted his father and he would tease Tim more.
Early, perhaps before the age of five, the possibility that a powerful person could humiliate him through teasing became established in Tim's emotional storage system.
Now twenty years later, Tim is a grown man.
He is well established.
Nobody tries to humiliate him, but if anyone teases him, he responds with immediate anger.
He cannot accept a good natured tease or joke.
So how is Tim to deal with this?
Clearly, he doesn't want to always get angry.
Sometimes afterwards, he feels, I shouldn't have done that.
I overreacted.
They didn't mean to hurt me, but it's not really in his control.

So this psychologist says the first step, of course, is to try to identify the trigger for his conscious self to know that this is a very important trigger for him and to try and understand its origin.
This isn't always easy.
He may need loving help from friends who can help him realize what it is that so forcefully arouses his anger.

Once equipped with that knowledge, the next step is for him to think about it, considering the fact that teasing can occur for other reasons, not just to humiliate him and to practice in his mind reevaluating what teasing is.
Next, he can begin to practice reshaping his response.
He may even sense when a teasing episode is about to occur and prepare himself before it happens so that over time, teasing can become a weaker emotional trigger for his anger.
I like that example, because I think when people have strong reactions to things that other people are just kind of like, huh?
Where did that come from?
It's just this change or this suggestion.
It's usually not the person who's offering the change or suggestion, nor is it the debilitating paranoia of the other person.
It's an emotional trigger.
Something from the past gets stirred up, and we paste it on the present.
We project it onto the present and say, here it is again.
It's always like this.
That makes for a pretty sad way of being, as I personally have experienced.
Circling back to that sixth grave precept, not discussing the faults of others, how do we as a sangha then address the differences of opinion we're all going to have?
How do we react to the rules of Zen, all its forms, its hierarchy?
This is one of the more rigorous forms of practicing Buddhism.
There's a lot of rules.
There is a hierarchy.

As I said, next week we're going to have an opportunity to all talk more about specifics, but maybe tonight I'd like to ask you just to consider the bigger picture of how we each cope with change and disagreements, how we talk to each other when something has been triggered in us.
Do we recognize our feelings as just that, just feelings, just thoughts that may be based in old experiences?
Or are we blind?
That's what I see this practice of immediate awareness is all about.

It's practicing awareness in every moment, and so when something comes up in a moment, I have to really pay attention to that and not get lost in this is the reality and it's just like it was before and it's going to be like this in the future and suddenly I'm way out of the present moment and I'm projecting a whole lot of fear into this triggering event, this triggering person, even just the triggering word.

I know this hasn't been a very long talk, but I guess I would like an opportunity if people would like to share a little bit of of how they look at, again, not specific issues within the Sangha, but just personally, how do we each deal with conflict?

One thing that I like to remember is some lines from the *Dhammapada*, when I'm getting all caught up and stressing out about something that I think is wrong and the lines from the *Dhammapada* are this: *What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday and our present thoughts build on our life for tomorrow.
Our life is a creation of our mind.

If a person speaks or acts with an impure mind, suffering will follow as the wheels of a cart follow the beast that pulls it.* I know it's been a short talk, but I think I was instructed to make sure I'm done by night, so I think I've got that down.
I guess I'd like to open it up to anybody who'd like to talk about this issue.
